title: How Logs Get Into a SIEM: Agents, Forwarding, Syslog and Parsing
intro: Log ingestion is the path that carries an event from the system that produced it into the SIEM's searchable store: collection, transport, parsing and indexing. This lesson teaches how that path is built, where it silently breaks, and how to onboard a new log source and prove that its events arrive intact and parsed.

sections.heading: The collection pipeline end to end
sections.content:
Every event you search in a SIEM has travelled through the same six stages, and a fault in any one of them looks, to the analyst, like the same thing: nothing happened. That is why ingestion matters more than any single detection. A perfect rule over an empty or mangled data set detects nothing.

| Stage | What happens | Typical failure | How it shows up |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Source | An OS, application or device writes an event (Security log, firewall syslog, cloud audit record) | Auditing not enabled, log too small and overwritten | The event never existed, so nothing downstream can find it |
| 2. Collection | An agent reads it locally, or the SIEM pulls or receives it without an agent | Agent stopped, wrong channel, credentials expired | Source goes quiet |
| 3. Transport | Bytes move to a collector or indexer over UDP, TCP or TLS | UDP loss, firewall block, TLS certificate expired | Gaps, bursts after reconnect, missing events |
| 4. Parsing and normalization | Raw text becomes named fields (src_ip, user, action) | No parser, wrong parser, format change after an upgrade | Events stored but fields empty |
| 5. Index and store | Events are written, compressed and retained | Disk full, licence cap hit, queue overflow | Events delayed or dropped at the edge |
| 6. Search | The analyst or a rule queries the store | Time range wrong, timestamps skewed | Events exist but are not found where expected |

A useful mental model is a plumbing system. The source is the tap, the agent is the first pipe fitting, the network is the long run of pipe, the parser is the filter that sorts what flows, and the index is the tank. If the tank is empty you do not stare at the tank; you walk the pipe backwards until you find the leak.

Two timestamps travel with every event and analysts confuse them constantly. Event time is when the thing happened on the source. Receive (or index) time is when the SIEM stored it. The difference is ingestion latency. In a healthy pipeline it is seconds; if it is minutes or hours, a rule that looks at the last five minutes will miss real activity, and an incident timeline built on receive time will be in the wrong order.

What matters to know: collection is not one product, it is a chain of independent components, often owned by different teams (Windows admins own the source, network engineers own the firewall rules, the SIEM team owns the collector). What matters to ask whenever a log source looks wrong: did the event get generated, did it leave the host, did it arrive, was it parsed, and is its timestamp correct? Answering those five questions in order isolates the broken stage in minutes rather than hours.

The rest of this lesson follows the pipeline in order. We will look at how collection is done on Windows and on network and Linux systems, how parsing turns text into evidence, what you should and should not collect, and how to keep the whole chain observable. The SIEM concept itself and detection writing are covered in other lessons; here the single concern is getting trustworthy data in.

sections.heading: Agent versus agentless collection and the common collectors
sections.content:
Collection comes in two shapes. With an agent, software installed on the source reads events locally and ships them. Agentless means nothing extra runs on the source: the source pushes events itself (syslog, an API webhook), or the SIEM reaches in and pulls them (WMI or RPC polling, an SSH session, a cloud API such as an S3 bucket of audit files).

| Aspect | Agent-based | Agentless |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Install footprint | Software on every host; needs deployment and patching | None on the source |
| Reliability | Local buffering, survives network outages, tracks position in the log | Push over UDP can lose events; pull depends on credentials and reachability |
| Filtering | Can drop noise at the source before it uses bandwidth | Usually everything is sent, filtering happens later |
| Security | Runs privileged; becomes attack surface and a target for tampering | Fewer binaries, but pull methods need a powerful remote account |
| Coverage | Only hosts where the agent is installed | Works for appliances, routers, SaaS where no agent is possible |
| Typical use | Windows and Linux servers, endpoints | Firewalls, switches, cloud services, legacy devices |

Neither wins universally. Servers and endpoints deserve an agent because you need buffering, filtering and tamper evidence. Appliances cannot run your agent at all, so syslog or an API is the only option. A mature estate uses both, and the analyst's job is to know which method a given source uses, because the failure modes differ.

The collectors you will meet most often:

| Collector | Platform | Transport | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Windows Event Forwarding (WEF) with a Windows Event Collector (WEC) server | Windows, built in | WS-Management over HTTP 5985 (Kerberos) or HTTPS 5986 | No third-party agent; the collector then forwards onward |
| WinCollect | QRadar, Windows | Syslog to an Event Collector, TCP 514 or TLS | Managed (central config) or standalone |
| Splunk Universal Forwarder | Windows, Linux, Unix | Splunk-to-Splunk on TCP 9997, optional TLS | Lightweight, persistent queue, indexer acknowledgement |
| Winlogbeat, Filebeat (Elastic Beats) | Windows, Linux | To Logstash (5044) or Elasticsearch (9200) | Reads event log channels and files, tracks position in a registry file |
| rsyslog, syslog-ng | Linux, Unix | UDP or TCP 514, TLS 6514 | Daemons that receive local and remote syslog and relay it |
| OpenTelemetry Collector | Cross-platform | OTLP over gRPC 4317 or HTTP 4318 | Vendor-neutral receivers, processors and exporters, common for cloud and application telemetry |

What matters to ask when you meet a new source: can I run an agent on it, what does the agent need (credentials, ports, a service account), what happens to events if the network is down, and where is the position bookmark stored? The last two questions decide whether an outage costs you minutes of delay or a permanent hole in the evidence.

sections.heading: Windows collection: WEF/WEC, WinCollect and choosing channels
sections.content:
Windows stores events in channels, named logs viewable in Event Viewer: Security, System, Application, and hundreds of operational channels such as Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational and Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational. Collection means choosing which channels to read and how to move them.

Windows Event Forwarding is built into the operating system. A source computer sends events to a Windows Event Collector server over WS-Management. There are two subscription types. In a collector-initiated subscription the collector pulls from a named list of sources, which is fine for a handful of servers. In a source-initiated subscription each client is told by Group Policy where the collector is and pushes by itself, which scales to thousands of machines. The Group Policy setting is Computer Configuration, Administrative Templates, Windows Components, Event Forwarding, Configure target Subscription Manager, with a value such as Server=http://wec01.corp.example.com:5985/wsman/SubscriptionManager/WEC,Refresh=60. Source computers need the Windows Remote Management service running; the collector needs the Windows Event Collector service enabled (wecutil qc) and WinRM configured (winrm quickconfig). The network service account on the source must be able to read the Security log, which is done by adding it to the Event Log Readers group.

The subscription holds an XPath query that filters at the source, for example only Security event IDs 4624, 4625, 4672, 4688, 4720 and 1102. Events land in the ForwardedEvents channel on the collector, whose default size is small; raise it, or it will overwrite events before your agent reads them. Delivery optimisation has three modes: Normal, Minimize Bandwidth and Minimize Latency. For security monitoring choose Minimize Latency so detections are not delayed by batching. Microsoft's guidance is roughly 4000 sources per collector, beyond which you add collectors.

WinCollect is IBM QRadar's Windows agent. Managed mode means the QRadar Console holds the configuration and pushes it to agents, so changing which channels are collected is a console operation; this is how you run hundreds of agents without touching each machine. Standalone mode keeps the configuration local on the host, useful for isolated networks without console access but painful to change at scale. WinCollect can collect locally on a server, or act as a remote poller that reads other Windows hosts, which is convenient but concentrates credentials and load on one box. It sends events to a QRadar Event Collector as syslog (TCP 514, or TLS). Always check the vendor's current support lifecycle before building a new design on any agent.

Why choose specific channels? The Security channel holds logons (4624 success, 4625 failure), privilege use (4672), process creation with command line (4688, if enabled), account changes (4720, 4728) and log clearing (1102). Sysmon adds what Security lacks: process creation with hashes and parent (event 1), network connections (3), image loads (7), process access such as LSASS reads (10), file creation (11) and DNS queries (22). PowerShell Operational adds script block text (4104), which exposes obfuscated commands that run in memory. A server collected only on Security tells you who logged on but not what malware did afterwards. Missing Sysmon is one of the most common reasons a real intrusion has no visible middle.

sections.heading: Network devices and Linux: syslog, transports, facilities and severities
sections.content:
Syslog is the common language of network devices and Unix systems. The current format is defined in RFC 5424; the older, looser BSD format in RFC 3164 is still sent by plenty of devices, which is a classic parsing headache. An RFC 5424 message looks like this:

    <34>1 2026-11-02T10:15:00.003Z fw01.corp.example.com sshd 4120 ID47 - Failed password for admin from 203.0.113.9 port 51022 ssh2

The fields are PRI, version, timestamp, hostname, application name, process ID, message ID, structured data (here a dash meaning none) and the message text. The number inside the angle brackets, PRI, packs two values: PRI = facility x 8 + severity. So 34 means facility 4 (auth) and severity 2 (critical), since 4 x 8 + 2 = 34.

| Severity | Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Emergency | System unusable |
| 1 | Alert | Act immediately |
| 2 | Critical | Critical condition |
| 3 | Error | Error condition |
| 4 | Warning | Warning |
| 5 | Notice | Normal but significant |
| 6 | Informational | Routine information |
| 7 | Debug | Debug detail |

| Facility | Name | Typical source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | kern | Kernel messages |
| 1 | user | User-level processes |
| 3 | daemon | System daemons |
| 4 | auth | Login and security |
| 10 | authpriv | Private authentication, such as sshd and sudo on many Linux builds |
| 16 to 23 | local0 to local7 | Free for applications and devices; firewalls and switches often use one of these |

Severity is the sender's opinion, not the analyst's. A firewall deny may be Informational while a failed admin login is Warning. Never filter on severity alone and assume you kept the important events.

Transport is where reliability is decided. UDP 514 is connectionless: there is no acknowledgement, no retransmission, and a busy collector or a congested link silently drops datagrams. Messages also may not exceed the datagram size, so long messages are truncated, and RFC 5424 only requires receivers to accept 480 octets while many accept 1024 or more. TCP 514 (or 601 in some conventions) gives ordered delivery and retransmission but a plain TCP connection can still lose whatever sat in the sender's memory when the link broke. TLS-protected syslog (RFC 5425, TCP 6514) adds encryption and mutual authentication, so nobody can read or inject events in transit; that matters for logs that carry usernames and addresses, and it prevents forged events reaching your SIEM.

On Linux, rsyslog and syslog-ng are the daemons. They read from journald or local files, apply filter rules by facility and severity, and forward to the SIEM. A single forwarding line in rsyslog, such as an action with type omfwd, target set to the collector, port 6514 and protocol tcp, is all it takes to start sending, which is both the convenience and the danger: it is easy to send and easy to forget to monitor.

What to ask about any syslog source: which transport, which port, which facility, which timestamp format and time zone, and is the sending IP the real device (a relay will hide it)? An analyst who sees a gap of exactly the busiest hour on a UDP source should suspect loss before suspecting an attacker.

sections.heading: Parsing and normalization: from raw text to evidence
sections.content:
A raw log line is just a string. A Windows 4625 event, a Linux sshd failure and a firewall deny all describe a failed or blocked connection, but each uses different words and different positions. Parsing extracts named fields from the raw text; normalization maps those names onto a common schema, so that source IP is called the same thing whether it came from a Cisco ASA or a Linux server. Every correlation, dashboard and detection rule runs on those fields.

Parsing is done in different places depending on the product. QRadar uses Device Support Modules (DSMs), prebuilt parsers per log source type, and custom properties for fields the DSM does not extract. Splunk assigns a sourcetype and applies field extractions and add-ons that map to the Common Information Model. Elastic uses ingest pipelines, Logstash filters and the Elastic Common Schema. OpenTelemetry uses processors and the log data model. Open schemas such as OCSF are emerging for the same purpose.

A grok pattern is a readable regular expression with names. For the sshd line from the previous section:

    Failed password for %{USERNAME:user} from %{IP:src_ip} port %{INT:src_port} %{WORD:protocol}

run against the message yields user=admin, src_ip=203.0.113.9, src_port=51022. The same event in Windows is already structured XML, where EventData contains TargetUserName, IpAddress and LogonType; the work there is mapping, not extraction.

What is the cost of an unparsed log? It is stored, so storage and licence are consumed, and it looks present on the source health page. But it is nearly invisible to analysis. Searches can only match words, not fields. A detection such as many failures for one user from one source never fires because the user and source fields are empty. A dashboard counting logons by country shows nothing for that source. Correlating a firewall event with an endpoint event through the shared IP fails. In QRadar these show up as events categorised Unknown or Stored; in other platforms as a generic sourcetype or a parse failure tag. The danger is that nothing errors: coverage looks green while the data is useless.

Parsing also breaks over time. A vendor changes the message format in a firmware upgrade, an app logs in a new language, or a new Windows version adds a field. Previously parsed events silently turn into unparsed ones the day after the upgrade. A related trap is the wrong parser: Linux logs accepted as a generic syslog source work but without authentication fields.

What to check for every new source: pick five known events (a successful login, a failed login, a policy change) and verify the fields you will rely on are populated with sensible values. Track the ratio of parsed to unparsed events per source, and treat a sudden rise as an incident in the pipeline itself. Normalization also hides one more problem: timestamp parsing. If the parser reads a local time as UTC, every event lands hours off, which the next section addresses.

sections.heading: What to collect: coverage, volume, licensing and time
sections.content:
You cannot detect what you do not collect. A technique is only visible if some log source records it, so coverage is the ceiling of your detection capability. If PowerShell script block logging is off, no rule can see an encoded payload; if Sysmon is missing, no rule can see a process access to LSASS. Conversely, collecting everything is not an answer, because volume costs money and drowns signal.

Licensing converts a technical choice into a budget. Some products license on events per second (EPS), others on gigabytes ingested per day. A rough calculation helps: at an average event size of 500 bytes, 1000 EPS is 500,000 bytes per second, about 43 GB per day. A single chatty source can double that. Windows Filtering Platform events (5156 and 5158) can generate thousands of events per host per hour; object access auditing (4663, 4662) on a file server can swamp everything else. When the licence cap is hit, products either queue, drop events or stop searching, usually in the middle of the busiest and most interesting period.

The discipline is to collect by purpose. Start from the questions you must answer and the techniques you must see, then choose sources and events:

- Identity: domain controller Security logs (4768, 4769, 4771, 4776), VPN and single sign-on logs.
- Endpoint: Security (4624, 4625, 4688 with command line, 4697, 7045), Sysmon, PowerShell 4104, EDR telemetry.
- Network: firewall allow and deny, DNS queries, proxy logs, DHCP leases (to map IP to host).
- Cloud and email: control-plane audit logs, mail gateway and mailbox audit.

Filter at the source where you can: an XPath query in a WEF subscription, a blacklist in a forwarder, a Sysmon configuration that excludes known-good, an rsyslog rule that drops debug severity. Filtering early saves bandwidth and licence, but each filter is a decision to be blind to something, so write it down and review it.

Time is part of the data. Detection correlates events across systems by timestamp, so every source must keep accurate time. Windows domain members take time from the domain hierarchy (the PDC emulator should sync to a reliable NTP source), Linux uses chrony or ntpd, and network devices need explicit NTP servers. Check three things: clock accuracy, time zone, and format. A firewall logging in local time without an offset, parsed as UTC, puts events hours into the future or past. Clock skew of even a minute reorders a fast attack chain: the process launch appears to occur after the network connection it caused, and a rule that joins events within a 30 second window fails. Best practice is to log in UTC, include the offset, and have the SIEM store event time and receive time separately.

What to ask: which attack techniques does this source let me see, what does it cost in volume, and is its clock right? Coverage reviews against a framework such as ATT&CK turn the first question into a map of gaps.

sections.heading: Operational concerns: buffering, back-pressure, duplicates and pipeline health
sections.content:
A pipeline that works on day one will break by month three, quietly. Operational maturity means expecting that, and designing so a failure costs delay, not evidence.

Buffering and queuing. When the network or the SIEM is down, a good agent keeps events and resumes. The Splunk Universal Forwarder has in-memory queues and optional persistent queues on disk; with useACK enabled it waits for the indexer to confirm receipt and resends if not, which converts at-most-once delivery into at-least-once. Winlogbeat has an in-memory queue and an optional disk queue, and records its position in a registry file. rsyslog uses action queues; setting queue.type to LinkedList with a queue.filename makes it disk-assisted, and syslog-ng offers disk-buffer. Plain UDP syslog has no buffer at all: if the receiver is not listening at that millisecond, the event is gone.

Back-pressure. If the destination is slower than the source, something must give. Options are block the producer, spill to disk, or drop. Blocking a firewall or a busy application because the log pipe is full can hurt production, so many designs choose drop for devices and disk-buffer for servers. Know which your pipeline does. A burst such as a port scan or an attack storm is exactly when volume peaks, which means pipelines fail when you need them most. Size for peaks, not averages.

Dropped events. Besides network loss, drops happen when the Security log is too small and wraps before the agent reads it (Windows default sizes are modest, so enlarge them), when a parser rejects malformed events, and when the SIEM exceeds its licence. Log clearing (1102 for Security, 104 for System) is itself an event worth alerting on, since attackers clear logs.

Duplicates and loops. Reinstalling an agent or deleting its position file can make it re-read the whole log and flood the SIEM with old events that look new (watch for receive time far from event time). Two overlapping subscriptions, or an agent plus a WEF feed on the same host, double count and break threshold rules. A loop occurs when a relay forwards to a collector that forwards back, or when the SIEM's own syslog output is sent to an input it reads; volume explodes until something falls over. Add a deduplication check and keep a diagram of who forwards to whom.

Monitoring the pipeline. Treat the pipeline as a system under monitoring:

- Silent source detection: alert if a source that normally sends events has sent none for a set period.
- Volume baselines: alert on sudden drops (broken) and spikes (flood or loop) per source.
- Latency: compare receive time with event time; alert if the median delay grows.
- Queue depth and agent status: forwarder queues filling, collector CPU, disk space.
- Parse health: unparsed ratio per source type.
- Inventory reconciliation: compare the SIEM's source list with the asset database (CMDB) to find hosts never onboarded.

A missing log source is a finding. Treat an agent that went offline at 02:00 on a domain controller as a possible tamper and ask the Windows team before assuming a patch window.

sections.heading: Worked example: onboarding a Windows server's Security and Sysmon logs
sections.content:
Scenario: a new Windows Server 2022 web server, WEB-SRV07, joins the estate. You must get Security and Sysmon events into the SIEM and prove they are arriving and parsed. This example uses a Splunk Universal Forwarder; the same steps apply with Winlogbeat, WinCollect or WEF with only the configuration syntax differing.

Step 1, make the source generate the right events. Confirm advanced audit policy for Logon, Process Creation, Account Management and Policy Change, and enable the setting Include command line in process creation events so that 4688 records the command line. Increase the Security log maximum size so it does not wrap in minutes.

Step 2, install Sysmon with an approved configuration (for example a community baseline tuned for your estate):

    sysmon64.exe -accepteula -i sysmonconfig.xml

Sysmon writes to Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational.

Step 3, install and configure the forwarder. In inputs.conf:

    [WinEventLog://Security]
    index = wineventlog
    disabled = 0
    start_from = oldest
    current_only = 0
    evt_resolve_ad_obj = 1

    [WinEventLog://Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational]
    index = sysmon
    disabled = 0
    renderXml = true

In outputs.conf point to the indexer on port 9997 with useACK = true. Open outbound TCP 9997 on the host firewall and the network path. Run the forwarder under a service account that can read the channels.

Step 4, verify at the source. Confirm the forwarder is connected (splunk list forward-server shows the indexer as active), and look in the forwarder's own log for connection errors. Confirm the channel has events: Get-WinEvent -LogName Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational -MaxEvents 5.

Step 5, generate known test events so you can recognise them: three failed logons with a wrong password (4625), then open a command prompt and run whoami (4688 and Sysmon event 1).

Step 6, verify at the SIEM. Search by host and count by channel and event code:

    index=wineventlog OR index=sysmon host=WEB-SRV07 | stats count by source, EventCode

You expect both sources present. Then check that fields are populated: for 4625, TargetUserName and IpAddress; for Sysmon 1, Image, CommandLine, ParentImage and Hashes. If you see raw XML in one blob and no fields, the sourcetype or add-on is missing. Check latency by comparing event time with index time; it should be seconds. Check that the host clock matches the SIEM (a skew shows up here immediately).

Step 7, close the loop. Add WEB-SRV07 to the monitored source list, set a silent-source alert for 15 minutes, record the filters and Sysmon config version, and note the expected daily volume so growth is noticed.

Outcome: an analyst can now answer who logged on, what ran, what it spawned and where it connected, from one host, with timestamps that line up with the firewall. Most onboarding failures are found in step 4 or 6: a blocked port, a missing channel permission, a disabled audit subcategory, or a parser that was never installed.

quiz.question: Your firewall sends syslog over UDP 514 to the SIEM. During a port scan the firewall logs spike, yet the SIEM shows far fewer deny events than the firewall's own console. What is the most likely cause and the best fix?

options.label: The parser is wrong; replace the DSM or sourcetype so that deny events are recognised
UDP datagrams are being dropped under load; move the feed to TCP or TLS syslog with buffering
The firewall clock is wrong; fix NTP so that events are not discarded as too old
The severity filter hides deny events; raise the severity threshold on the firewall

quiz.explanation: UDP syslog has no acknowledgement, retransmission or buffer, so a burst that overruns the receiver or a congested link silently loses datagrams, and the loss is largest exactly when volume peaks. Moving to TCP or TLS syslog (TLS on 6514) gives ordered, retransmitted delivery and a sender-side queue. A wrong parser would leave the events present but with empty fields, not fewer events. Clock error shifts timestamps and does not make a SIEM discard events. Raising a severity threshold would remove even more events, the opposite of the fix.

quiz.question: A new Windows server's Security events appear in the SIEM, and a search shows plenty of 4625 events, but the dashboard counting failed logons by user and source IP shows nothing for this server. What should you check first?

options.label: Whether the licence has been exhausted, which stops the dashboard from reading data
Whether the server's Security log is large enough to hold a day of events
Whether the events were received twice because the agent was reinstalled
Whether the events are parsed, with user and source address fields populated, under the correct parser

quiz.explanation: Events that are searchable by text but absent from a field-based dashboard are the signature of missing or wrong parsing: the dashboard groups by user and source IP fields, which are empty if extraction failed. Checking sample events for populated fields and the assigned sourcetype or DSM is the direct test. Licence exhaustion would affect all sources and usually stop ingestion, not just this dashboard. Log size would create gaps in the data, but the events are present. Duplicates would inflate counts rather than remove them.

quiz.question: You design Windows collection for 3000 servers and want no third-party agent, with central control through Group Policy. Which approach fits, and which setting keeps detection latency low?

options.label: Source-initiated Windows Event Forwarding to a Windows Event Collector, using the Minimize Latency delivery mode
Collector-initiated subscriptions listing all 3000 servers by name, using Minimize Bandwidth mode
WinCollect in standalone mode on each server, configured by hand on every host
Plain UDP syslog from the Windows servers to the SIEM on port 514 for all channels

quiz.explanation: Source-initiated WEF is built into Windows, is pointed at the collector by Group Policy so clients push on their own, and scales to thousands of machines; Minimize Latency stops batching from delaying events that detections need. A collector-initiated subscription naming every server does not scale well, and Minimize Bandwidth deliberately batches and delays. WinCollect is a separate agent, and standalone mode means manual per-host configuration, the opposite of central control. Windows does not natively emit its event channels as UDP syslog, and UDP would be unreliable even if it did.

quiz.question: After a reinstall of the forwarder on a busy server, the SIEM shows a large burst of events whose event times are two weeks old but whose receive times are today, and thresholds fire repeatedly. What explains this and what is the right response?

options.label: The attacker replayed old logs; isolate the host and begin incident response immediately
The agent lost its position bookmark and re-read the log from the start; confirm and deduplicate or exclude the replayed range
The server clock jumped back two weeks; reset the SIEM time zone to match
The collector was overloaded by a loop; disable the host's firewall to relieve it

quiz.explanation: Agents track their read position in a bookmark, registry or checkpoint file; deleting it or reinstalling can make the agent re-read the channel from the oldest event, so old events arrive with current receive times and trip count-based rules. The right response is to confirm by comparing event and receive time, then suppress or deduplicate the replayed range. Replayed old data is a pipeline artefact long before it is evidence of attacker replay, so full incident response is premature. A clock jump would change event times to the future or past of new events, not produce a two week old burst, and changing the SIEM time zone does not touch it. A loop produces repeated identical volume, and disabling a firewall is never a fix.

quiz.question: A syslog message arrives starting with <86>. Using PRI = facility x 8 + severity, what do the facility and severity mean, and what does that tell you about the source?

options.label: Facility 8 (uucp) and severity 6 (informational), so it is a routine UUCP message
Facility 10 (authpriv) and severity 6 (informational), so it is a private authentication message such as sshd or sudo
Facility 11 (ftp) and severity 6 (informational), so it is a routine FTP transfer message
Facility 4 (auth) and severity 54 (debug), so it is an unusual debug entry from a login service

quiz.explanation: Dividing 86 by 8 gives 10 remainder 6: facility 10 is authpriv and severity 6 is informational. This is typical of sshd and sudo records on many Linux systems, so it is exactly the authentication evidence you want parsed. Facility 8 would give a PRI of 70 to 71 for severity 6 or 7 and not 86. Facility 11 with severity 6 would be 94. Severity cannot exceed 7, so a value of 54 is impossible, and facility 4 would give a PRI between 32 and 39.
